statements.claim: Krishna showed Arjuna the great capital of Magadha as the three brothers approached: filled with flocks and herds, its water never failing, adorned with fine mansions in excellent array, free from every kind of calamity, and said 'We shall, however, by slaying him today, humble his pride.'
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21 (Ganguli): Vasudeva's speech to Partha is nearly verbatim, including 'We shall, however, by slaying him to-day humble his pride.'

statements.claim: The five hills of Girivraja — Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri and the delightful Chaitya — seemed jointly to protect the city; Chaitya was worshipped by the citizens and by the royal line of Vrihadratha.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: hills named exactly; Chaitya 'worshipped by the race of Vrihadratha, as also by the citizens'. The 'fingers of a cupped hand' simile is connective imagery.

statements.claim: Instead of entering by the gate, the brothers tore down the Chaityaka peak at the point where the great drums of Vrihadratha used to sound — drums which, once beaten, sounded for a full month.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: arriving at the gate the brothers (instead of passing through it) broke down the high Chaityaka peak worshipped by the Magadhas, at the point where Vrihadratha's drums (made from the cannibal Rishava's hide) 'once beaten their sound lasted one full month'.

statements.claim: In the guise of Brahmanas, bare arms as their only weapons, the brothers walked the crowded streets past shops of edibles and wreaths, snatched garlands from the flower-vendors, their sandal-smeared arms like the trunks of sala trees, passed through three crowded gates proudly like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds, and the people of Magadha wondered much at the giants.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: every element near-verbatim (guise of Brahmanas, bare arms as only weapons, garlands snatched from flower-vendors, sala-trunk arms, three crowded gates, Himalayan lion simile, the Magadhas' wonder).

statements.claim: Within the city the learned Brahmanas had seen evil omens and reported them to Jarasandha; his priest made the king mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him, and the king began a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts to ward off the portents.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: near-verbatim sequence.

statements.claim: Jarasandha rose up in haste and received the strangers with water for the feet, honey and the ingredients of the arghya, and gifts of kine, bidding them welcome; Bhima and Arjuna remained silent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'Jarasandha rising up in haste received them with water... honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya--with gifts of kine... Ye are welcome'; 'both Partha and Bhima remained silent'. Krishna speaking for them is carried from the chain (DKS_0166).

statements.claim: After the welcome Jarasandha censured the guests for coming into his city by no proper gate.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'When Jarasandha censures the disguised guests for entering by an improper gate'; the passage itself truncates just as Jarasandha addresses them, and Krishna's reply presupposes the question.

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'These are the rules of the ordinance... an enemy's abode should be entered through a wrong gate and a friend's abode through the right one... this also is our eternal vow that having entered the foe's abode for the accomplishment of our purpose, we accept not the worship offered to us.'
statements.evidence: Pack source excerpt (MBh 2.21) quotes the reply near-verbatim.

statements.claim: The brothers' refusal of the offered worship meant the king's courteous welcome was over: they had declared themselves his enemies, and what remained was the purpose for which they had come (slaying him).
statements.evidence: The 'untouched water and gifts' are a visual dramatization of the vow just quoted (we accept not the worship offered); the framing of the exchange as a declaration of enmity is narrative consequence, not a new sourced fact.

notes: Highly faithful to MBh 2.21; Krishna's reply quoted nearly verbatim. The passage's hermitage digressions (Gautama, Nagas) are omitted without distortion.

statements.claim: Jarasandha asked why the guests, whom he had never injured even on careful scrutiny, regarded him, an innocent man, as a foe, demanding a true answer 'for this is the rule followed by the honest.'
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: Jarasandha's opening speech is near-verbatim (the source's vocative 'ye Brahmanas' is dropped, as their disguise is not yet broken in the story).

statements.claim: Krishna replied that he came not of his own will: a certain person at the head of a royal line had sent him and his companions; and that Jarasandha had brought many Kshatriyas of the world as captives to his city — a wicked wrong by which he could not regard himself innocent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: 'there is a certain person of the head of a (royal) line... At his command have we come against thee. Thou hast brought, O king, many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives (to thy city.) Having perpetrated that wicked wrong how dost thou regard thyself as innocent?'

statements.claim: Krishna said the captive kings were being treated with cruelty and kept for sacrifice to the god Rudra; slaughter of human beings as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen, and Jarasandha was addressing persons of his own order as animals fit for sacrifice (to god Sankara).
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: near-verbatim, including 'slaughter of human being as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen... sacrifice unto god Sankara...' and Rudra as the intended recipient.

statements.claim: Krishna revealed their identity: 'Know that we are certainly not Brahmanas. I am Hrishikesha, otherwise called Sauri, and these two heroes among men are the sons of Pandu. O king of Magadha, we challenge thee. Fight standing before us. Either set free all the monarchs, or go thou to the abode of Yama.'
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: quoted nearly verbatim (source spells 'Hrishesha').

statements.claim: Krishna spoke of warriors dying in open fight attaining heaven as the sure consequence — the triumph won by Indra through vanquishing the Asuras — and of kings Damvodhava, Kartavirya, Uttara and Vrihadratha who met destruction with all their forces for disregarding their superiors; valour dwells in every man, so Jarasandha should cast off superiority and pride before his equals.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: content near-verbatim (heaven as the certain consequence of death in battle, Indra's triumph over the Asuras, the four ruined kings, 'Valour dwelleth in every man').

statements.claim: Jarasandha answered unshaken: he never made a captive of a king without first vanquishing him; all the monarchs in his city were defeated in open war; it is the Kshatriya duty to bring others under sway by prowess and treat them as slaves; having gathered the monarchs for sacrifice he would not liberate them from fear; he offered combat — troops against troops, or alone against one, two or three.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: Jarasandha's reply near-verbatim; the passage truncates mid-sentence at 'or against two, or against three' but the pack summary and corpus render the same challenge.

statements.claim: The lord Sauri, ever devoted to truth, keeping in view the command of Brahma and remembering that the ruler of Magadha was destined to be slain in battle by Bhima and not by a descendant of Madhu, desired not to slay the king himself; he drew back his own hand and left the king to Bhima.
statements.evidence: Pack source excerpt (MBh 2.22): 'the lord Sauri ever devoted to truth ... keeping in view the command of Brahma and remembering that the ruler of Magadha was destined to be slain in battle by Bhima and not by the descendant of Madhu (Yadavas), desired not to slay himself king Jarasandha.'

statements.claim: Krishna alone would have been more than a match for the king of Magadha, and the strength of the descendants of Madhu could have ended the matter there and then.
statements.evidence: Rhetorical framing of Krishna's restraint; the pack states only that he desired not to slay Jarasandha (the sentiment that he could have is implied, not stated).

statements.claim: The son of Pandu stepped forward to meet Jarasandha, and the long duel began — a fight in which Krishna took no part because this death was destined to be Bhima's.
statements.evidence: Bridge to the ensuing fight: the pack passage truncates at Jarasandha's reply, but the duel follows directly from the excerpt's statement that Jarasandha was destined to be slain by Bhima; the 'long duel' itself is not narrated in the quoted excerpt.

notes: Faithful to MBh 2.22; Krishna's and Jarasandha's speeches nearly verbatim. All claims check out; no contradictions with the pack.

statements.claim: Muchukunda, waking after sleeping through the turning of eras, walked out into the daylight and, beholding men of diminished stature, knew that the Kali age had arrived.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24 (Wilson): 'beholding men of diminutive stature, now first knew that the Kali age had arrived.'

statements.claim: Muchukunda praised Krishna as the sovereign of all things, the eternal lord, Hari, and Krishna granted his wish, promising: 'Go to whatever celestial regions you wish... When you have fully enjoyed all heavenly pleasures, you shall be born in a distinguished family, retaining the recollection of your former births; and you shall finally obtain emancipation.'
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: the boon speech is quoted nearly verbatim; the opening clause 'Thus praised by the wise Muchukunda' underlies the story's 'praised by the wise'.

statements.claim: Muchukunda prostrated himself before the lord of the world, went out from the cave, and departed to Gandhamadana, the shrine of Nara-Narayana, to perform penance.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: 'prostrated himself before Achyuta, the lord of the world, Muchukunda, went forth from the cave... departed to Gandhamádana, the shrine of Narańáráyańa, to perform penance.'

statements.claim: In time it came about exactly as Krishna had promised: Muchukunda enjoyed the celestial regions, was born again in a distinguished family with his memory of former births intact, and at last obtained emancipation.
statements.evidence: Proleptic closing consistent with the boon Krishna states verbatim in the passage; the pack's excerpt does not itself narrate the later fulfillment (which the corpus chain places ahead of this point).

statements.claim: Krishna, having destroyed his enemy by stratagem, returned to Mathura, took captive Kalayavana's army — rich in horses, elephants and cars — conducted it to Dwaraka and delivered it to Ugrasena; the Yadu race was relieved of all fear of invasion.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: near-verbatim ('Krishńa having by this stratagem destroyed his enemy, returned to Mathurá, and took captive his army, rich in horses, elephants and cars, which he conducted to Dwáraká, and delivered to Ugrasena, and the Yadu race was relieved from all fear of invasion').

statements.claim: Balarama, hostilities having ceased, went to Nanda's cow-pens desiring to see his kinsmen, and conversed with the herdsmen and their women with affection and respect: the elders embraced him, he embraced the younger ones, and with those of his own age he talked and laughed; the cowherds made him many kind speeches.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: near-verbatim, including the embrace pattern and the cowherds' kind speeches to Halayudha.

statements.claim: Some gopis spoke to Balarama with the affectation of anger and jealousy, asking after Krishna — 'Is all well with the fickle and inconstant Krishna?... Does the volatile swain, the friend of an instant, amuse the women of the city by laughing at our rustic efforts (to please him)? Does he ever think of us...? Will he not come here once again to see his mother?' — and adding 'Father, mother, brother, husband, kin, what have we not abandoned for his sake?... it is a different tale to tell for him without us, and for us without him.'
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: gopis' speech is near-verbatim, including the rhetorical questions and the closing lament.

statements.claim: Balarama carried the gopis' message back with him when he left the cow-pens.
statements.evidence: Closing connective; the passage ends with the gopis' speeches and does not narrate Balarama's departure or what he carried back.

notes: Faithful retelling of VP 5.24 (Wilson); dialogue near-verbatim. The story's one forward-looking fulfillment sentence is consistent with the quoted boon.

statements.claim: Kamsa's widows Asti and Prapti, daughters of Jarasandha, came to their father's court and told him of their widowhood; grief and anger rose in Jarasandha.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.1-2 (pack rendering): 'Kamsa's widows Asti and Prapti went to their father Jarasandha and told him of their widowhood; enraged...'; HV 1.89: Jarasandha heard of Kamsa's death from his two daughters and was worked up with anger.

statements.claim: Jarasandha owed Kamsa a debt: the dead king had been his son-in-law and ally — the son of Ahuka who, chaining his own father, ruled Mathura depending on Jarasandha's help and disregarding the Yadavas; and when the vicious-souled Kamsa was slain by Rama and Krishna, Ugrasena, encircled by the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, became king in his place.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: near-verbatim, including Kamsa chaining his father, ruling 'depending on Jarāsandhā's (help) and disregarding the Yadavas', the debt Jarasandha wished to pay, and Ugrasena's accession 'encircled by Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas'.

statements.claim: Kamsa had been the one man who held the Yadava race in check while Jarasandha gathered the world's kings into his prisons.
statements.evidence: Kamsa's check on the Yadavas is inferred from HV 1.89 (he ruled with Jarasandha's backing, disregarding the Yadavas); Jarasandha's imprisonment of captive kings is carried from the corpus chain (MBh 2.22, DKS_0168 pack: 'many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives').

statements.claim: Resolved to make the earth free of Yadavas and burning like fire in anger, Jarasandha made every possible arrangement and started for Mathura in no time.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.1-2 (pack rendering: 'he resolved to make the earth Yadava-free'); HV 1.89: 'burning like fire in anger... making every possible arrangement the king of Magadha started for Mathurā... to slay all the Yadus.'

statements.claim: All the highly energetic warrior kings defeated and subjugated by Jarasandha's prowess, and all his friends, relatives, kinsmen and allies, followed him with their own armies, eager to please him, out of jealousy toward Janardana.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: 'All the highly energetic warrior kings who were defeated and subjugated by Jarāsandha's prowess, all those who were his friends, relatives, kinsmen and allies, encircled by their own armies, followed Jarāsandha with a view to please him... out of jealousy towards Janārddana.' The 'fear' motive added in the story is a connective gloss on their subjugation.

statements.claim: Among the kings who followed were Dantavakra of Karusha, the powerful king of Chedi, the king of Kalinga, Bhishmaka and his son Rukmi, the kings of Anga and Vanga, of Koshala, Kashi and Dasharna, Bhagadatta the lord of the Yavanas, Suvala of Gandhara, and Duryodhana with the other sons of Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: the roster is listed nearly verbatim (Dantavakra the king of Karusha, king of Chedi, king of Kalinga, Bhishmaka, his son Rukshmi, kings of Anga and Vanga, kings of Koshala, Kashi and Dashārna, Bhagadatta the lord of Yavanas, Suvala the king of Gāndhāra, Duryodhana and other sons of Dhritarāshtra).

statements.claim: The allied host entered the province of Shurasena, a country abounding in barley and fuel, and the command went out for the armies of the united kings to lay siege on all sides to the city of Mathura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: 'Entering the province of Shurasena, abounding in barley and fuels, they all... laid siege to Mathurā'; HV 1.90 excerpt: 'Let the armies of the kings united lay siege on all sides to this city.'

statements.claim: Twenty-three akshauhinis — counted in soldiers, horses, chariots and elephants — surrounded Mathura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.3 (Sanskrit: akṣauhiṇībhir viṃśatyā tisṛbhiś cāpi saṃvṛtaḥ = surrounded by twenty-three akshauhinis) and v.7 (bhaṭāśva-ratha-kuñjaraiḥ). Note: HV 1.89 counts six divisions at the outset; the story follows its primary source (BP) at the siege.

statements.claim: Krishna saw that host like an overflowing sea and reflected long — the blessed Hari, kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ, one whose humanity is an instrument for his work in the world.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.4-5 (Sanskrit): 'nirīkṣya tad-balaṃ kṛṣṇa udvelam iva sāgaram / cintayām āsa bhagavān hariḥ kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ'. The gloss of kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ follows standard commentary.

statements.claim: The fires of the besieging host burned through the first night, and Krishna was still thinking, because he had come to act in human ways and a human king must first decide what he is willing to do.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close; Krishna's reflection is sourced (v.5) but the night-fires and the 'human ways' deliberation are narrative framing of that reflection.

notes: Faithful blend of BP 10.50.1-5 (primary) with HV 1.89/1.90 roster and siege details. HV's six-division figure vs BP's twenty-three akshauhinis is a source variant; story follows BP. VP 5.22's 'eighteen times' variant not asserted here.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had come to avenge his son-in-law Kamsa, resolved to leave no Yadava alive — the twenty-three divisions camped around Mathura like a sea overflowing its banks.
statements.evidence: Recap carried from the immediate chain: BP 10.50.1-5 (DKS_0170 pack): widows' report, rage, 'make the earth Yadava-free', twenty-three akshauhinis; the 'sea overflowing its banks' simile is BP 10.50.4 verbatim.

statements.claim: Reflecting on the host, Krishna thought: 'I will destroy this force... this weight that has been heaped upon the earth. It was to remove the earth's burden that I came down; and for the protection of dharma, another form of mine is ever maintained.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.6-9 (Sanskrit): haniṣyāmi balaṃ hy etad bhuvi bhāraṃ samāhitam... etad-artho 'vatāro 'yaṃ bhū-bhāra-haraṇāya me / anyo 'pi dharma-rakṣāyai dehaḥ saṃbhriyate mayā.

statements.claim: Out of the empty air above Mathura two chariots descended, bright as the sun, each with its driver at the reins and carrying ancient divine weapons — bows, quivers, maces, armor — coming of their own accord, unsummoned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.10-11 (Sanskrit): ākāśāt sūrya-varcasau... āyudhāni ca divyāni purāṇāni yadṛcchayā; pack rendering: 'two chariots with the splendor of the sun descended from the sky with drivers and ancient divine weapons'. yadṛcchayā = spontaneously, grounding 'of their own accord'.

statements.claim: Krishna turned to Balarama: 'Look, Arya... Calamity has come upon the Yadavas, who look to you. It was for this that we two were born — to bring ease to the good.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.12-13 (Sanskrit): paśyārya vyasanaṃ prāptaṃ yadūnāṃ tvāvatāṃ prabho / etad-arthaṃ hi nau janma sādhūnām īśa śarma-kṛt.

statements.claim: The brothers armed themselves and the two chariots rolled out through the gates of Mathura, out onto the open ground between the walls and the enemy host.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.14 (Sanskrit): daṃśitau rathinau purāt (the two, armed, chariot-borne, from the city). The citizens running into the streets are connective colour.

statements.claim: Krishna's chariot was driven by Daruka; as the wheels cleared the gate he raised the great conch to his lips and blew it once, the sound rolling across the plain between city and camps.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.15 (Sanskrit): śaṅkhaṃ dadhmau vinirgatya harir dāruka-sārathiḥ — Hari, whose charioteer was Daruka, having gone out, blew his conch.

statements.claim: Terror entered the hearts of the Magadha king's forces and the allied kings' ranks at the conch's sound.
statements.evidence: Pack rendering of BP 10.50.6-15: 'Krishna blew his conch and terror entered the enemy's hearts.' The trembling soldiers' vignette is elaboration of that terror.

statements.claim: Two chariots stood before the greatest army of the age, and for a moment the army did not move; then the battle began.
statements.evidence: Closing bridge to DKS_0172; the pause before battle is dramatic connective consistent with the narrative flow, not a sourced beat.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.50.6-15 (primary, Sanskrit verses rendered accurately); opening recap and closing bridge are connective. Daruka's role and the 'of their own accord' detail both match the Sanskrit.

statements.claim: Seeing the brothers come, Jarasandha shouted abuse — insults for Krishna, and for Balarama a challenge: if he had any courage, to come and fight, summoning his fortitude.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.16-17 (Sanskrit): tāv āha māgadho vīkṣya he kṛṣṇa puruṣādhama... tava rāma yadi śraddhā yudhyasva dhairyam udvaha — the Magadha addresses Krishna with abuse (puruṣādhama) and dares Rama to fight with fortitude.

statements.claim: On the towers, terraces and gates of Mathura, the city's women gathered to watch and swooned, overcome with grief at the sight of the enormous host.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.20 (Sanskrit): striyaḥ purāṭṭālaka-harmya-gopuraṃ samāśritāḥ sammumuhuḥ śucārditaḥ — women, resorting to the city's ramparts, palaces and gates, swooned, afflicted with grief.

statements.claim: Krishna's arrows streamed out without pause or gap, like a wheel of fire burning in an unbroken circle; elephants with split foreheads fell, horses fell with necks severed, chariots were smashed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.21-23 (Sanskrit): nirantaraṃ yadvad alāta-cakram (without interval, like a wheel of fire); nirbhinna-kumbhāḥ kariṇo nipetur (elephants with split frontal lobes fell); aśvāḥ śara-vṛkṇa-kandharāḥ (horses with necks severed by arrows).

statements.claim: Jarasandha's army was an ocean, dark and without a shore, one no one could have crossed; the one who waded into it, though he fought in mortal form, was not measured by mortal measure.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.27-28 (Sanskrit): balaṃ tad aṅgārṇava-durga-bhairavaṃ duranta-pāraṃ... tathāpi martyānuvidhasya varṇyate — the army like a frightful, uncrossable ocean, yet the crossing is described of him who conforms to mortal ways.

statements.claim: In the sky, out of sight of the armies, gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, saints and Yakshas gathered from all quarters to watch, and the field shone under their gathered light like the night sky lit with luminaries.
statements.evidence: HV 1.92 (in pack): 'there came there from all quarters thousands and thousands of gods Gandharvas, Siddhas, Saints and Yakshas. Shining greatly in their effulgence the battle-field looked like welkin covered with luminous bodies.'

statements.claim: In the middle of it all Balarama sought out Jarasandha, who had spent his chariot, horses and charioteer and stood chariotless on the field; with his army slain and allies gone, the king was bound with ropes by the Vrishni soldiers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.29-30 (Sanskrit): jagrāha virathaṃ rāmo jarāsandhaṃ mahā-balam (Rama seized the chariotless, mighty Jarasandha); badhyamānaṃ hatārātiṃ pāśair vāruṇa-mānuṣaiḥ (being bound with divine and human ropes after his enemies were slain); v.33 hateṣu sarvānīkeṣu (all his armies slain).

statements.claim: Balarama seized Jarasandha the way a lion seizes a lion, by the shoulders, so that the king hung helpless in his grip.
statements.evidence: The lion-seizing-lion simile is in the pack excerpt (BP 10.50.29), but the 'by the shoulders' grip and 'hung helpless' are dramatizing gestures of the same supported seizure; no source specifies the body part.

statements.claim: Krishna stayed the binding: 'The Magadha is not to be slain... He will gather forces again.' He spoke to the captive with words of pure and plain meaning, and released him.
statements.evidence: Pack rendering of BP 10.50.16-41 (Krishna stayed the binding, 'The Magadha is not to be slain; he will gather forces again'); v.32 vākyaiḥ pavitrārtha-padair (with words of pure meaning). HV 1.92 corroborates the sparing via the celestial voice (the king of Magadha is not to be slain by Rama).

statements.claim: Released by the two lords of the world, Jarasandha stood in shame — a shame softened by being counted worthy of such handling by the heroes — then turned and walked off the field, and no one stopped him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.31 (Sanskrit): sā mukto loka-nāthābhyāṃ vrīḍito vīra-sammataḥ — released by the two lords of the world, ashamed, approved/held worthy by heroes.

statements.claim: The people of Mathura poured out through the gates to meet Krishna, free of their fever and carried on a wave of joy; conches and kettledrums (dundubhis, bheris, turyas) sounded from the walls; the streets were sprinkled with water and adorned with banners; women on the rooftops showered the returning chariots with garlands, curds and unbroken rice.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.35-38 (Sanskrit): māthurair upasaṅgamya vijvarair muditātmabhiḥ; śaṅkha-dundubhayo nedur bherī-tūryāṇy anekaśaḥ; sikta-mārgāṃ hṛṣṭa-janāṃ patākābhir abhyalaṅkṛtām; nicīyamānaḥ... mālya-dadhy-akṣatāṅkuraiḥ (showered with garlands, curds and unbroken grains).

statements.claim: The weapons that had come down from the sky for the battle were seen no more, as if they had never been.
statements.evidence: HV 1.92: 'And all the weapons that came down from the welkin also disappeared.'

statements.claim: Seventeen times after that day Jarasandha came again to Mathura, each time with an army reckoned in akshauhinis, and seventeen times the Vrishnis, by Krishna's splendor, destroyed his host and sent him home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.40-41 (Sanskrit): evaṃ saptadaśa-kṛtvas tāvaty akṣauhiṇī-balaḥ / akṣiṇvaṃs tad-balaṃ sarvaṃ vṛṣṇayaḥ kṛṣṇa-tejasā — seventeen times, with an army of that many akshauhinis, the Vrishnis destroyed his whole force by Krishna's splendor. (VP 5.22's 'eighteen times' is a variant the story does not use; BP is the primary source.)

statements.claim: The king who had sworn to leave no Yadava alive was spared by the very men he had come to destroy — spared, as he himself suspected, for a purpose none of them could yet see.
statements.evidence: Closing suspense-framing: the sparing and its purpose (Jarasandha's eventual death by Krishna's own means) are sourced (BP 10.50.31; HV 1.92 divine voice), but the attribution of suspicion to Jarasandha himself is the narrator's gloss, not in the sources.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.50.16-41 with HV 1.92 corroboration; Sanskrit verses rendered accurately (wheel-of-fire arrows, lion seizure, seventeen attacks, celebration scene). The single embellished gesture (seizure 'by the shoulders') is connective.

statements.claim: Gargya, preceptor of the Andhaka and Vrishni races, had kept the vow of celibacy all his life — he had a wife but had never known her — and his brother-in-law mocked him before the king and named him impotent.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'The high-minded Gārgya was the preceptor of both the Andhaka and Vrishni races. He always observed the vow of celibacy; and although he had a wife he did not know her... this brother-in-law described him as impotent before the king.'

statements.claim: Stung by the dishonor, Gargya left the city, gave up thought of his wife, and for twelve years lived on pounded iron and worshipped Mahadeva the trident-holder, until the god granted a boon: an all-powerful son who would discomfit the descendants of the Vrishni and Andhaka races in battle.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'having been thus dishonored in the city of Ajitanjaya and giving up his desire of being united with his wife... living on pounded iron for twelve years he worshipped Mahādeva, the holder of trident. For this Rudra conferred on him a boon that he would obtain an all powerful son who would be able to discomfit in battle the descendants of the Vishni and Andhaka races.'

statements.claim: The sonless king of the Yavanas heard of the boon, brought Gargya to his own kingdom and set women (milk-women) to attend on him; the Apsara Gopali, taking the form of a milk-woman, conceived through him; the child was Kalayavana, raised in the palace like the king's own son, and he reigned when the king died.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'The king of Yavanas had no son. Hearing of the boon... the king brought him over to his own kingdom... engaged the milk-women to attend him... an Apsara, Gopāli by name, conceived that dreadful and undecaying embryo through Gārgya... brought up in the inner appartment, like his son... after the demise of the lord of Yavanas Kalyavana became king.'

statements.claim: The kings of the Shakas and Tukharas, the Daradas, Paravas and Tanganas, the Khashas and Panhavas — hundreds of mlechcha kings from the lands near the great mountains — took shelter under Kalayavana.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'Shaka, Tukhāra Darava, Parava, Tangana, Khasha, Panhava and hundreds of Mlechcha kings, living near Himavan, took shelter under him.' (Story's spellings follow the VP 5.23 variant roster of the same kings.)

statements.claim: When Kalayavana finally marched on Mathura, his host covered the earth like a swarm of locusts and the dust raised by his soldiers hid the path of the sun.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'Encircled by those Dasyu kings resembling a swarm of locusts... the king of Yavanas set out for Mathura... The path of the sun was covered with the dust raised by the soldiers.'

statements.claim: Krishna, having heard from Narada the story of the boon, had never met the Yavana head-on; now he told his kinsmen the calamity that had befallen the Vrishnis and Andhakas — the enemy could not be slain by them because of the trident-holder's boon; he had tried conciliation and the rest but the proud king wanted battle; Narada had told him 'You are to live here'; Jarasandha did not forgive and the kings sheltering under him were displeased over Kamsa's death; they would never prosper if they stayed in Mathura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: Krishna's speech to his kinsmen is near-verbatim ('Great is the calamity... enemy is unslayable by us on account of the boon... I employed all other means as conciliation etc... he wishes for battle worked up with pride. 'I am to live here:' this Nārada said to me... The emperor Jarāsandha is not forgiving... on account of the distruction of Kansa, have been displeased... we will never acquire prosperity if we live in this city.'); the 'never met head-on' derives from 'took no notice of Kālayavana... because he had heard from Narada the story of his obtaining the boon'.

statements.claim: Krishna sent an envoy to Kalayavana with a sealed jar containing a dreadful black serpent, saying 'Krishna is like a deadly serpent'; Kalayavana, understanding the threat, filled the jar with innumerable sharp-beaked ants, which devoured the serpent and reduced it to ashes.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: near-verbatim (black serpent 'resembling a collection of collyrium' sealed in a jar; the envoy's words; Kalayavana filling the jar with dreadful ants that ate the serpent and reduced it to ashes).

statements.claim: Kalayavana knew Krishna by the marks Narada had described — the chest marked with Shrivatsa, the Kaustubha jewel on his neck, the ever-glad face, the pure smile — and, certain no other could be he, ran at him; Krishna turned and fled toward the cave though the Yavana shouted 'Flight is not proper for one born in the Yadu clan!'
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.1-8 (Sanskrit): śrīvatsa-vakṣasaṃ... kaustubhāmukta-kandharam... nitya-pramuditaṃ... su-kapolaṃ śuci-smitam; lakṣaṇair nārada-proktair nānyo bhavitum arhati; iti niścitya yavanaḥ prādravad taṃ parāṅ-mukham; palāyaṇaṃ yadu-kule jātasya tava nocitam.

statements.claim: Inside the mountain cave Kalayavana found a man lying asleep, laughed — 'This one has led me far... and now lies here like a virtuous man, pretending to sleep' — and, certain it was Krishna, kicked him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.9 (Sanskrit): nanv asau dūram ānīya śete mām iha sādhu-vat; VP 5.23: 'concluded it must be Krishńa, and kicked him'; pack rendering: 'the fool kicked the sleeping man thinking him Krishna'.

statements.claim: The sleeper — Muchukunda — had been asleep for a very long time; slowly he opened his eyes, and the angry glance that fell on the Yavana burned Kalayavana to ashes in a moment.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.10-11 (Sanskrit): sa utthāya ciraṃ suptaḥ śanair unmīlya locane... dṛṣṭi-pātena; VP 5.23: 'casting on him an angry glance, the Yavana was instantly consumed, and reduced to ashes'; HV 1.114: 'he looked at the Yavana king with angry eyes. As soon as he was eyed, the king of Yavanas was all ablaze.' The motives imputed to the glance (anger at being woken/kicked) are connective glosses on the sourced angry glance.

statements.claim: Krishna entered the cave only after being pursued by an army that no one in the world could defeat, and the pursuit was exactly what he intended.
statements.evidence: The flight before the pursuing Yavana is sourced (BP 10.51.5-6: the Yavana ran at him, feeling him within reach at every step), but 'the pursuit was exactly what Krishna intended' is narrative inference from the luring stratagem.

notes: Faithful blend of HV 1.114 (Gargya origin, tribal kings, serpent ruse — near-verbatim), BP 10.51.1-11 (recognition marks, cave pursuit) and VP 5.23 (kick and burning glance). All named tribes and details check out against the pack.

statements.claim: The sleeper was Muchukunda, son of Mandhata, of the Ikshvaku line — a king of an age long since passed.
statements.evidence: Pack rendering of BP 10.51.12-20: 'Muchukunda, son of Mandhata of the Ikshvaku line, guarded the gods in battle against the asuras.'

statements.claim: Long ago, when the gods fought the asuras, the hosts of heaven led by Indra asked this mortal king to stand guard for them; Muchukunda fought for the gods in their war and guarded them through battles longer than the lives of ordinary men.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.13-15 (Sanskrit): sa yācitaḥ sura-gaṇair indrādyair ātma-rakṣaṇe (he was asked by the hosts of gods led by Indra for their own protection). The 'battles longer than ordinary lives' is dramatization of the ages-long guard duty summarized in the pack.

statements.claim: When the war was over, the gods released him, telling him gently that the world he had left was gone: his kingdom, with its enemies cut down, no longer waited for him, and his sons, queens, kinsmen, ministers and counselors were all gone; 'Time is mightier than the mighty' and 'The Blessed Lord is the immutable sovereign.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.16-18 (Sanskrit): nara-lokaṃ parityajya rājyaṃ nihata-kaṇṭakam / sutā mahiṣyo bhavato jñātayo 'mātya-mantrinaḥ / kālo balīyān balināṃ bhagavān īśvaro 'vyayaḥ — leaving the world of men, your kingdom with its thorns cut down; your sons, queens, relatives, ministers and counselors; time is mightier than the mighty; the Blessed Lord is the immutable Sovereign.

statements.claim: The gods offered Muchukunda a boon, as promised: 'Choose whatever you wish... Ask anything except liberation — that is not ours to grant.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.19 (Sanskrit): varaṃ vṛṇīṣva bhadraṃ te ṛte kaivalyam adya naḥ — choose a boon, good fortune to you, except kaivalya (liberation), which is not ours to give. The 'as promised' is a connective reference to the gods' earlier undertaking.

statements.claim: Muchukunda bowed to the gods and asked for sleep — not for a night or a season, but to lie down in the earth and sleep without waking, undisturbed, until the proper time came round for him to wake; the gods granted it and he lay down in the cave and slept.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.20 (Sanskrit): evam uktaḥ sa vai devān abhivandya mahā-yaśāḥ (thus addressed, the greatly glorious one bowed to the gods) — continuing in the pack's rendering: 'he chose sleep as his boon and lay in the cave'; his sleeping through ages is carried from DKS_0173 (BP 10.51.10, ciraṃ suptaḥ).

statements.claim: The years turned to ages and ages to yugas while Muchukunda slept: kingdoms rose and fell, Mathura was besieged and delivered, and a king came to his cave and was burned to ash at his feet.
statements.evidence: Recap-connective: the burned king is Kalayavana (DKS_0173, BP 10.51.10-11) and Mathura's siege and deliverance are the chain events of DKS_0170-72 (BP 10.50); the yuga-scale passing of time is framing consistent with the ages-long sleep.

statements.claim: The gods asked Muchukunda to guard them because he was strong and because a king of the Ikshvaku line who gave his word kept it.
statements.evidence: Motivation added by the narrator; the pack states only that he was asked (yācitaḥ) to guard the gods, not why.

statements.claim: When Muchukunda woke, he understood without being told that the one who had woken him was not the one who had kicked him, and he opened his mouth to ask who the stranger was.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting connective leading into the next beat (DKS_0175); consistent with the previous story's events (BP 10.51.1-11, VP 5.23) but not itself a sourced fact.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.51.12-20; the boon offer and the gods' speech match the Sanskrit closely. Backstory recaps and closing scene-setting are connective. Subtitle matches the pack summary.
